concept.name: Liquidity risk
concept.definition: The risk of being unable to fund increases in assets or meet obligations as they come due without incurring unacceptable losses (funding liquidity), or of being unable to exit positions at prevailing prices without moving the market (market/asset liquidity). BCBS principles treat its management as paramount because one institution's shortfall can have system-wide repercussions.
concept.intuition: Liquidity risk is the risk that you need cash or an exit right now and the market charges you ruinously — or does not trade at all.
concept.mechanics: Banks manage it through liquidity buffers, stress tests, contingency funding plans, and limits on maturity transformation; for traders it shows up as widening spreads, thinning depth, and slippage, typically spiking together with volatility and funding stress in self-reinforcing liquidity spirals.
concept.formula: No single formula; measured through liquidity coverage of obligations under stress (survival horizon) and market-side metrics such as bid-ask spread and market depth.
concept.failure_modes: Liquidity evaporates exactly when most needed: haircuts and margins rise, buyers vanish, and fire-sale prices make 'liquid' portfolios behave as illiquid. Models calibrated to normal-market depth systematically underestimate liquidation cost in stress.
concept.misconceptions: An asset that trades tight spreads in calm markets is not 'liquid' in the risk sense — liquidity is regime-dependent — and solvency does not protect against liquidity failure, since solvent-on-paper institutions can still collapse from a funding run.
concept.example: In 2007-08, banks that assumed contingent funding would always be available discovered that 'liquidity can evaporate and illiquidity can last for an extended period of time,' necessitating central bank support (BCBS).

citations.source: BCBS: Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision
